<p style="font-weight: bold; font-size: 24px;">
Statistical analysis of oceanographic data (Black Sea – Danube area)
</p>


This project aimed to understand **how environmental conditions influence species distribution**. Using oceanographic data, I applied **statistical analyses** (normality tests, clustering, PCA, biodiversity indices) to identify spatial patterns. Results showed that nutrient-rich, silty environments near the Danube support higher biodiversity, while more distant sandy areas host different communities.The complete script is available below. 

**Skills acquired**: 

- Statistical analysis (Shapiro test, data transformation)

- Biodiversity indices (Shannon, Simpson, evenness)

- Multivariate analysis (PCA, clustering)

- Distance metrics (Bray-Curtis, Hellinger, Chord)

- Data visualization (maps, dendrograms, PCA plots)

- Ecological data interpretation (species–environment relationships)

        width="65%" height="750px"

::: {.scroll-box}
```{r}
#| eval: false

#Statistical analysis of oceanographic data (Black Sea – Danube area)

#Sample of the code used in this analysis

## 1. Data Import
#The datasets used in this analysis include species data, environmental variables, #and station information. They are imported and cleaned before analysis.

Especes <- read_excel("~/Desktop/master oceano/M2/Maths/Marilaure/Exam janvier/Especes.xlsx")
View(Especes)
Especes <- Especes[-c(2, 3, 25, 26),]

FullData <- read_excel("~/Desktop/master oceano/M2/Maths/Marilaure/Exam janvier/FullData.xlsx")
View(FullData)
FullData <- FullData[-1, ]

data_spc <- read.table("~/Desktop/master oceano/M2/Maths/Marilaure/Exam janvier/BiomassDominantSpecies.txt", header=TRUE, sep="\t")
data_env <- read.table("~/Desktop/master oceano/M2/Maths/Marilaure/Exam janvier/EnvData.txt", header=TRUE, sep="\t")
data_station <- read.table("~/Desktop/master oceano/M2/Maths/Marilaure/Exam janvier/Stations.txt", header=TRUE, sep="\t")


## 2. Data Preprocessing
#Data were cleaned and formatted. Some rows were removed and variables were #converted to numeric format when necessary, while keeping spatial variables #unchanged.

exclude_cols <- c("Depth", "latitude", "longitude", "Station")

FullData[] <- lapply(FullData, function(x) {
  if (!any(names(x) %in% exclude_cols)) {
    as.numeric(x)
  } else {
    x
  }
})

Especes[] <- lapply(Especes, function(x) {
  if (!any(names(x) %in% exclude_cols)) {
    as.numeric(x)
  } else {
    x
  }
})


## 3. Normality Analysis of Environmental Variables
#The distribution of environmental descriptors was assessed using histograms and #Shapiro-Wilk tests. When necessary, transformations were considered to improve #normality.

hist(data_env$Porosity, main="Histogramme de la Porosité", xlab="Porosité", freq=FALSE, col="lightblue")
abline(v = c(mean(data_env$Porosity),median(data_env$Porosity)), col=c("green", "blue"), lty=c(2,2), lwd=c(3, 3))
shapiro.test(data_env$Porosity)

hist(data_env$Grain, main = "Histogramme du Grain", xlab= "Grain", freq = FALSE, col = "lightblue")
abline(v=c(mean(data_env$Grain), median(data_env$Grain)), col= c("green", "blue"), lty=c(2,2), lwd=c(3,3))
shapiro.test(data_env$Grain)


## 4. Biodiversity Indices
#Several biodiversity indices were calculated to describe species diversity at each #station:
#- Species richness (N0)
#- Shannon index (H)
#- Hill numbers (N1, N2)
#- Evenness indices (J, E1, E2)

N0 <- rowSums(data_spc > 0)
H <- diversity(data_spc)
N1 <- exp(H)
N2 <- diversity(data_spc, "inv")
J <- H/log(N0)
E1 <- N1/N0
E2 <- N2/N0

div1 <- data.frame(N0, H, N1, N2, E1, E2, J)
div1


## 5. Spatial Distribution of Biodiversity
#The spatial distribution of biodiversity indices was visualized using geographic #coordinates (latitude and longitude). Point size and color represent biodiversity #levels.

ggplot(biodiv_map, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, size = N1, color = N1)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +  
  geom_text(aes(label = Station), hjust = -0.3, vjust = -0.5, size = 4, color = "black") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(3, 10)) +  
  scale_color_gradient(low = "blue", high = "gold") +  
  theme_minimal()
  
  
## 6. Distance Matrices
#Distance matrices between sites were computed using different metrics:
#- Bray-Curtis distance
#- Chord distance
#- Hellinger distance
#These metrics allow comparison of sites based on species composition and #environmental variables.

spe.db <- vegdist(d.spe)
spe.dbL <- vegdist(decostand(d.spe,'log'))
spe.dc <- dist(decostand(d.spe,'norm'))
spe.dh <- dist(decostand(d.spe,'hel'))

coldiss(spe.db)
coldiss(spe.dbL)
coldiss(spe.dc)
coldiss(spe.dh)


## 7. Cluster Analysis
#Hierarchical clustering was performed to group sites based on similarity. Several #clustering methods were compared:
#- Single linkage
#- Complete linkage
#- Average linkage (UPGMA)
#- Ward method
#The best method was selected using cophenetic correlation and silhouette analysis.

spe.norm2 <- decostand(d.spe2,'norm')
spe.dist2 <- dist(spe.norm2)

spe.dist.average2  <- hclust(spe.dist2, method= "average")
plot(spe.dist.average2)


## 8. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) – Species Data
#A PCA was performed on species data to identify patterns in species distribution #across stations.

spe.pca <- rda(spe.hel)
summary(spe.pca)

biplot(spe.pca, scaling=1)
biplot(spe.pca, scaling=2)


## 9. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) – Environmental Variables
#A PCA was conducted on environmental variables to identify major environmental #gradients influencing the system.

env.pca <- rda(d.env.sc)
summary(env.pca)

biplot(env.pca, scaling=1)
biplot(env.pca, scaling=2)


## 10. PCA on Biodiversity Indices
#A PCA was performed on biodiversity indices to explore relationships between #diversity metrics and identify patterns among stations.

env.pca <- rda(d.bio.valid)
summary(env.pca)

biplot(env.pca, scaling=1)
biplot(env.pca, scaling=2)
```

<p style="font-weight: bold; font-size: 24px;">
Internship in Stable Isotope Analysis
</p>



This internship focused on the **ecophysiology of the Antarctic sea star *Odontaster validus*** through stable isotope analysis. I was responsible for preparing biological samples (grinding, acidification, and encapsulation) to ensure accurate **isotopic measurements**. I also gained insight into isotopic techniques and the functioning of **EA-IRMS instrumentation**. This experience strengthened my laboratory skills, scientific rigor, and understanding of trophic ecology in marine ecosystems.

**Skills acquired**: 

- Sample preparation for stable isotope analysis (grinding, acidification, encapsulation)

- Handling of laboratory equipment and chemical safety procedures

- Understanding of stable isotope ecology (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N, δ³⁴S)

- Knowledge of isotopic fractionation and tissue turnover concepts

- Familiarity with EA-IRMS instrumentation and analytical workflow

**Valorisation of marine resources**

This project provides a **strategic analysis of the Thai fisheries and aquaculture sector**, with a focus on **shrimp production**. It examines production trends, the diversification of exploited species, and the organization of the value chain, while integrating economic, environmental, and social dimensions. Using a **One Health approach**, it addresses challenges such as overfishing, disease outbreaks, global market competition, and **links between production, food security, and health**. The study also evaluates **public policie**s and **sustainability strategies**, proposing pathways for a more resilient, quality-oriented, and environmentally responsible development of the sector.

**Skills acquired**: 

- Sectoral data analysis (fisheries & aquaculture)

- International market research

- Strategic analysis (SWOT)

- Systems thinking & One Health approach

- Environmental and sustainability assessment

- Public policy and economic analysis

<p style="font-weight: bold; font-size: 24px;">
The Hidden Side of Oil Spills
</p>


**Oil spills** represent massive releases of hydrocarbons into the marine environment, with ecological impacts depending on the chemical composition of the oil, the affected ecosystem, and local physicochemical conditions. Hydrocarbons, particularly **Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon (PAHs)**, can disperse, sediment, or **bioaccumulate**, affecting marine life from phytoplankton to mammals. **Chemical dispersants** accelerate oil fragmentation but may increase its **toxicity** to organisms. **International regulations** and local measures (sorbents, barriers, animal care) help mitigate impacts, yet risk assessment remains complex. Prevention and management of oil spills require a thorough understanding of hydrocarbon chemistry, marine ecology, and remediation techniques.

**Skills acquired**: 

- Environmental Chemistry & Toxicology (hydrocarbon composition, behavior, toxicity, including PAHs)

- Marine Ecology & Ecosystem Impact Analysis 

- Pollution Mitigation & Remediation Techniques (dispersants, sorbents, skimmers, and cleanup strategies)

- Regulatory & Risk Assessment Skills (international conventions, local regulations and environmental risk evaluation)

- Scientific Research & Communication

<p style="font-weight: bold; font-size: 24px;">
Biochemistry and Physiology of Marine Animals (Collaborative Project)
</p>

This academic project explores the **biochemistry and physiology of marine animals**, focusing on the adaptations of **blue-ringed octopuses** (genus Hapalochlaena). It examines their **evolutionary origins**, habitat distribution, feeding strategies, reproductive behavior, and **advanced camouflage systems**. Particular attention is given to their unique use of **tetrodotoxin (TTX)**, a powerful neurotoxin used for both predation and defense. This work highlights how morphological, physiological, and behavioral traits are finely tuned to environmental constraints.

**Skills acquired**: 

- Scientific research and literature review

- Data synthesis and critical analysis

- Academic writing in English

- Team collaboration

- Marine biology and biochemistry knowledge

- Oral and written scientific communication
